extracted.intended_audience: researchers preparing and submitting ERC grant proposals (prospective ERC applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Explains the ERC's seven-phase evaluation process and the criteria used at each stage (allocation, remote review of B1/B2, panel meetings, interviews) so applicants can prepare Part A, B1 and B2 accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel expertise and interdisciplinarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The panel members are the most important element of the evaluation process. They are top specialists in their field, and they are able to work as generalists. Do not forget that the ERC panels are very interdisciplinary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels are selected by the Scientific Council, work on alternate years (with ~25% renewal each call), and each panel member typically receives 20–45 proposals. Panel composition and interdisciplinarity affect how proposals are read and discussed; you should therefore write for expert readers who must also act as generalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest rules and excluded reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel members are contacted to address any type of conflict of interest; this may exclude them from reviewing a proposal and/or from being present in the room when a proposal is discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical COI reasons: same host institution, past collaboration, rivalry, mentorship relationships. Applicants may nominate up to “3 excluded reviewers”; if a panel member is on that list they will leave the room. ERC asks panel members for details on expertise months before deadline to spot conflicts early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate Part A (abstract, descriptors, keywords) for preliminary allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary allocation of proposals to panel members is done using information in part A of your proposal (your abstract, the descriptors, and the keywords you have provided). At this point the ERC does not have access to B1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because panel chairs assign (typically) 4 panel members per proposal based on Part A, ensure your abstract, descriptors and keywords accurately reflect the proposal to obtain appropriate reviewers and correct panel assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-panel/call for secondary panel (panel transfer) assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicants have called a secondary panel (a.k.a cross-panel review), the panel chair assesses if this is really necessary and is allowed to ask for a panel transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel transfer occurs only after careful discussion between two panel chairs to ensure fairness. Use secondary panel requests only when the proposal genuinely lies outside the primary panel's expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of scientific integrity, open access, and unconscious bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel chairs meet with the ERC president who gives an overview highlighting important topics for the Scientific Council members: scientific integrity, open access, unconscious bias, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These high-level issues are part of the governance/oversight of the review process and may surface during chair-level discussions; ensure your proposal complies with ERC expectations on integrity and open access policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility focus in Part B1 (project synopsis, CV, track record)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first remote phase, panel members read at home only part B1 of the proposal, which includes the project synopsis, your CV, and your track record. They are asked to focus on feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because panel members read many proposals (20–45), present a clear, compelling, and easy-to-read B1 that demonstrates feasibility. The page links to additional guidance on how to write B1; use that guidance and make reviewers' lives easy and excited about the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring (1–5) of project and applicant during remote review
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel members must write a review for each proposal and mark the project and the applicant on a scale of 1 to 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants do not see these numeric scores, but other panel members do; scores are used to compile a ranking list provided at the start of the step 1 meeting. Written reviews are shared (scores are not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 decision bands (A/B/C) and progression rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Through discussion the panel calibrates itself and finally decides which people they want to see for an interview. Proposals that score an A will automatically proceed to step 2; those that score a B or a C are rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants receive a panel comment and all written reviews (without scores). There is a 1-month window to submit a redress, but redress is limited to procedural mistakes (scientific disagreement with reviews is not a valid ground).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative shortlisting: 'maximum 3x the budget' constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one administrative restriction rule: 'maximum 3x the budget'. Proposals whose collective budget is 3x the budget that the panel will eventually allocate will make it to step 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This budgetary cap is used to equalize chances across panels: even if a proposal scores well, progression to interviews is constrained by the panel's aggregated shortlisted budget (roughly limited to 3× the eventual allocation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and role of remote reviewers; importance of a clear abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: After step 1, panel members suggest remote reviewers (around 12 suggested, with the ERC contacting them to obtain at least 3 remote reviewers). When reviewers are invited, they decide if they are the right people for the job based solely on your abstract (they don’t see your name).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is very important that your abstract is clear and well written so the ERC can recruit appropriate remote reviewers. Statistics show the number of remote reviewers is not correlated with success; what matters is getting the right experts to accept the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology evaluation in the second remote phase (B2)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the second remote phase, which takes place between step 1 and 2 panel meetings, panel members and remote reviewers receive both parts of the proposal, part B1 and B2. In this remote phase, they look at methodology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a rigorous, detailed methodology in B2 demonstrating feasibility and the ability to execute the project. Remote reviewers (expert referees) will scrutinize methods and are key to informing the panel discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final interview and A/B funding decision at Step 2
rubrics_metrics.description: After each applicant’s interview, the panel has to decide whether the proposal will get an A or a B. An A means that the proposal should be funded if an unlimited budget were available. B means that even if there was an unlimited budget, this proposal should not be funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the top 'A' proposals are funded. The interview is crucial: panels discuss each proposal in depth (around 1.5 hours per proposal by the whole panel in addition to remote review). Prepare to discuss science clearly and defend feasibility and methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of redress (appeal) after Step 1
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants will receive the decision of the panel in the form of a panel comment as well as all the reviews without the scores. Applicants have 1 month to redress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Redress is allowed only for procedural mistakes by the ERC; scientific disagreement with reviewers' critiques is not grounds for redress. Use the feedback to improve future applications even if funding is not awarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and conciseness to help overloaded reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel members read between 20–45 proposals, so get them excited about your idea and make their life as easy as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write succinctly, highlight the key contributions and feasibility early (especially in the abstract and B1), and structure information so busy reviewers can quickly grasp significance and approach.
